About: Faraday's law two ways: a ring moving past a magnet at rest, and a magnet moving through a ring at rest

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the track from x = −14 to 14 cm seen obliquely from above, drawn at one scale, with the 3.0 cm wire ring, the bar magnet (north end red) and faint lines of its field. Eight charges sit on the ring: grey arrows are their velocity when the ring moves; blue arrows are the magnetic force per unit charge v × B along the wire, orange arrows the electric field E. From question 5 on, a dashed circle of the same size at x = −6 cm marks a closed path with no wire; it carries E arrows when there is an electric field there. All force arrows share one fixed scale (key at top right). The key is drawn flat to the screen, but the arrows lie in the tilted plane of the ring, so in this oblique view they look shorter than the key at the same value, by up to about half depending on where they sit round the ring; the Readouts give the exact values. Right: ΦB and ℰ against d, the current run solid and the previous completed run faint and dashed, each labelled with what moved.
Controls
What moves picks the ring or the magnet and returns the run to d = −12 cm. Run starts the motion (or resumes it after Pause); Pause holds the bodies and the traces; ⏮ Rewind returns the moving body to d = −12 cm, keeps the last completed run as the faint trace and clears the current one. The moving body always goes at 4.0 cm/s, so a run from d = −12 to 12 cm takes 6.0 s.
Measured
d is the magnet's centre relative to the ring's centre, positive once it has passed through. ΦB comes from the dipole's vector potential round the wire, ℰ = −dΦB/dt at the current d, and the forces per unit charge are taken along the wire in the sense of ℰ, so 2πa times their sum is ℰ. The values are in the Readouts panel below the Controls; the two forces per unit charge appear from question 2 on.

Guided Inquiry

1 · What pushes the charges

The ring is set to move: it starts 12 cm from the magnet, which sits at the middle of the track with its north pole towards the ring. Before pressing Run, predict what pushes the charges of the ring along the wire as the ring slides towards the magnet.

2 · The emf as the ring passes

Keep the settings of question 1. Before pressing Run, predict the trace of the electromotive force ℰ in the right-hand plot as the ring passes over the magnet, from d = −12 cm to d = 12 cm.

3 · Now the magnet moves

Now the magnet moves. The ring sits at the middle of the track and the magnet starts 12 cm away, moving towards it at the same 4.0 cm/s, and the trace of the run with the ring moving stays faint. Before pressing Run, predict the trace of ℰ.

4 · The force on the charges

Keep the settings of question 3. Before pressing Run, predict the readout of the magnetic part of the force per unit charge along the wire, and what drives the charges round the ring.

5 · The empty circle

Keep the settings of question 3. Before pressing Run, predict what the dashed circle, where there is no wire, shows as the magnet passes through it.

6 · The empty circle, ring moving

The ring moves again, starting from d = −12 cm, and the magnet is at rest. Before pressing Run, predict what the dashed circle shows as the ring slides over the magnet.

7 · Same emf, two explanations

The emf in the ring depends only on the relative motion: ℰ = −dΦB/dt is the same whichever body moves.

The explanation depends on the frame. When the ring moves, the magnetic force v × B on its moving charges does the pushing. When the magnet moves, the changing B brings a circulating electric field, present even in empty space and not conservative.

Moving the Ring or Moving the Magnet

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A wire ring and a bar magnet sit on a track. In one run the ring slides over the magnet, in the other the magnet slides through the ring, always at 4.0 cm/s. The sim records the flux through the ring, the emf in it, and the push on the charges in the wire.

What you'll learn

  • How the flux and the emf depend on where the magnet is.
  • What pushes the charges round the wire in each run.
  • What happens on a closed path where there is no wire.
  • How the sign of the emf follows Lenz's law.
The sim's layout, drawn schematically: the track on the left, the two plots on the right.

What's on screen

  • The ring: a wire loop of radius a = 3.0 cm, with eight charges on it.
  • The magnet: north end red, south end blue.
  • Grey arrows: the velocity of the charges, when the ring moves.
  • Blue arrows: the magnetic force per unit charge, v × B, along the wire.
  • Orange arrows: the electric field E along the wire.
  • Dashed circle: a path of the ring's size at x = −6 cm with no wire on it.
  • Scale key (top right): 100 µN/C, drawn flat to the screen. The blue and orange arrows lie in the tilted plane of the ring, so they look shorter than the key at the same value; the Readouts give the exact values.
  • Plot lines: ΦB and ℰ against d. Solid is the current run, faint dashed the last completed one.
See itLook at the opening setup. Watch for: the magnet in the middle of the track and ΦB reading 0.30 µWb at d = −12.00 cm.

Fixed in the sim: the moving body always goes at v = 4.0 cm/s, so the run from d = −12 to +12 cm takes 6.0 s. d is the magnet's centre relative to the ring's centre, positive once it has passed through. The magnet is a point dipole of 1.0 A m², and the ring's own current is ignored. The pushes per unit charge are taken along the wire in the sense of ℰ, so 2πa times their sum is ℰ.

03

The flux depends only on d, so ℰ comes in two pulses of opposite sign

Whichever body moves, the flux through the ring depends only on d. The sim takes the flux from the vector potential of the magnet's dipole round the wire, and the flux rule of notes section 7.2 gives ℰ = −dΦB/dt, with d changing at v. In closed form, for the sim's dipole μ and ring radius a:

The flux is the first formula. Its rate of change, with d increasing at v, is the second.

ΦB peaks at 20.94 µWb at d = 0, where it is not changing, so ℰ = 0 there. ℰ is largest at d = ±a/2 = ±1.5 cm, reaching −23.98 µV at d = −1.5 cm and +23.98 µV at d = +1.5 cm: two pulses of opposite sign. Nothing in the formulas says which body moves, so the two runs trace the same curves.

ΦB and ℰ against d from the formulas above. The sim's plots show the same curves.
Key idea. The emf follows the rate of change of the flux, not the flux itself: it is zero at the flux peak.
See itWatch d run from −4 cm to +4 cm. Watch for: ℰ dipping to −23.98 µV, back to 0 at d = 0, then rising to +23.98 µV, while ΦB peaks at 20.94 µWb.
See itPut the magnet’s centre in the plane of the ring, d = 0. Watch for: ΦB at its peak of 20.94 µWb and ℰ at 0.00 µV.
04

With the ring moving, the magnetic force on its charges does the pushing

When the ring slides, its charges move with it at v. The part of B along the track is parallel to v and gives no force. The part Bs that spreads outward across the wire does, and v × B points along the wire. This is the flux rule for a loop moving in a static field (notes eq. 7.15):

Bs is the component of B pointing outward from the axis, at the wire.

At d = −1.5 cm, Bs = 3.18 mT, so v Bs = 4.0 cm/s × 3.18 mT = 127.2 µN/C. Times 2πa = 18.85 cm, that is 23.98 µV, the ℰ of the formula above. At d = 0 the outward part Bs is zero, and so is the push.

Moves d

These controls move the sim too. Choose the magnet to follow the next section.

Key idea. With the ring moving, v × B along the wire is the emf per unit length: 2πa times it is ℰ.
See itPut the moving ring at d = −1.5 cm. Watch for: the magnetic push at −127.2 µN/C, the electric push at 0.0, and ℰ at −23.98 µV.
05

With the magnet moving, an electric field does the pushing

Now the ring is at rest, so its charges are at rest, and the magnetic force q v × B on them is zero. A force on charges at rest is by definition an electric force, so the changing B must be accompanied by an electric field E (notes section 7.2). At d = +1.5 cm the sim reads a magnetic push of 0.0 and an electric push Eφ = +127.2 µN/C, the same as v Bs for the moving ring at that d.

Looking along the axis, from the side away from the magnet, at d = −1.5 cm: the same push round the ring, 127.2 µN/C, in the same sense.

Faraday's law (notes eq. 7.16) gives the emf round a loop at rest from this field:

The flux rule holds for a loop at rest too, with E in place of v × B.

So ℰ matches the moving-ring run at every d. Why the two descriptions agree lies in the relativity of electric and magnetic fields, which the notes do not treat.

Key idea. The push round the ring is the same in both runs. Only its name changes: v × B for the moving ring, E for the moving magnet.
See itSwitch to the moving magnet and go to d = +1.5 cm. Watch for: the magnetic push at 0.0, the electric push at +127.2 µN/C, and the solid trace lying on the faint dashed one of the ring run.
06

The electric field exists on an empty circle as well

Faraday's law holds for any closed path, wire or not. The dashed circle at x = −6 cm has the ring's radius and no wire on it. With the magnet moving, E arrows still run round it, all the same way at any moment.

Its strength depends on how far the magnet is from the circle. It is 0 when the magnet's centre is in the circle's plane, at d = −6 cm, and largest, 127.2 µN/C, 1.5 cm either side, with opposite senses. With the ring moving instead, the magnet is at rest, B changes nowhere, and the dashed circle shows no arrows.

Left: the track with the empty path at x = −6 cm. Right: the field on it as the magnet passes.

Round a loop that encloses changing flux the line integral of E is not zero, so this E is not conservative and is not the gradient of any potential. In differential form (notes eq. 7.21):

Key idea. The electric field belongs to the changing magnetic field, not to the wire.
See itMove the magnet’s centre across the plane of the dashed circle. Watch for: the orange arrows on the dashed circle shrinking to nothing at d = −6 cm and coming back pointing the other way round.
See itLook at the same pass with the ring moving, at d = −1.5 cm. Watch for: blue arrows on the ring and none on the dashed circle.
07

Lenz’s law sets the sign of ℰ

As the north pole approaches, the flux through the ring, measured away from the magnet, increases. The induced current gives the ring a magnetic moment μ pointing back at the magnet, and the force on that dipole pushes the ring away: the ring is repelled and whoever moves it works against that force (notes Fig. 65). In Elihu Thomson's jumping ring, an aluminium ring on the iron core of a coil is thrown upward in the same way when the current is switched on.

After the notes' Fig. 65, with the sim's magnet and ring.

In the sim the sign shows in ℰ. While d is negative the flux is growing and ℰ is negative. At d = +1.5 cm the flux is the same 14.99 µWb as at −1.5 cm but falling, and ℰ is +23.98 µV.

Key idea. The minus sign in ℰ = −dΦB/dt means the induced current opposes the change in flux.
See itPut the ring at d = +1.5 cm. Watch for: ΦB at 14.99 µWb, as at d = −1.5 cm, and ℰ at +23.98 µV.
08

Summary

In one line. A ring and a magnet pass each other; the sim shows the flux, the emf and what pushes the charges, for each body in turn.

Common mix-ups

  • "The emf is largest when the flux is largest." At d = 0 the flux peaks at 20.94 µWb and ℰ is 0. ℰ is largest, 23.98 µV in size, at d = ±1.5 cm.
  • "The ring is at rest, so nothing pushes its charges." An electric field does, 127.2 µN/C at d = +1.5 cm, as v × B did for the moving ring.
  • "The magnet moves the other way on screen, so the signs flip." Only d enters: ℰ at d = −1.5 cm is −23.98 µV in both runs.
  • "An electric field needs a wire or charges to exist." It is there on the empty dashed circle, up to 127.2 µN/C.

Things to try on your own

  • Run the ring, press Run again for the magnet, and compare the solid and faint traces.
  • With the magnet moving, watch the dashed circle as d passes −6 cm.
